Chapter 25

The shell: a root that knows nobody

The root layout has no header and no load; the (site) group has both; the header computes its links in a {const} declaration tag and reads scrollY from svelte/reactivity/window; view transitions in onNavigate; a version banner from updated.current; two error pages sharing one view.

By the end of this chapter

Arrange layouts so that prerendered pages and per-request pages can coexist, and know what belongs at the root and what does not.

The layout split is the decision this chapter is about, and it came from a failure. The first version had the header in the root layout, fed by a root +layout.server.ts that loaded the signed-in person. Then the guides were prerendered, and a prerendered page is rendered once, at build time, with nobody signed in — and that answer is baked into its data. A signed-in person navigating to a guide would see “Sign in” in the header. So the root knows nobody, and the pages that need to know live in a group.

Two more things in that block belong to every page. afterNavigate asks the browser to look for a new service worker on each client-side navigation, because the browser only looks by itself on a full page load, and a tab left open across a deploy would otherwise keep the old worker for as long as it stays open — chapter 39 explains the worker and why the check is skipped with no network. And the last thing in the script is one line in onMount: a data-hydrated attribute on the root element. onMount in the root layout runs once the whole tree has hydrated, so the attribute is an honest signal that the JavaScript is running — a stylesheet can hide a control that needs it until then, and the end-to-end suite waits for it in the test that proves text typed *before* hydration survives (chapter 34).

What is left at the root is what every page shares: the fonts and stylesheet, the toaster, the deploy banner, and the two navigation hooks. onNavigate wraps the completion of every client-side navigation in document.startViewTransition, so the old page cross-fades into the new — and an element with a view-transition-name, like the trip title, morphs. Unless the person prefers reduced motion: then no transition is started at all. Turning the CSS off is not enough, because the browser’s own default for a view transition — a 250ms cross-fade, and a position-and-size morph of every named element — runs unless something replaces it; not starting the transition is the one switch that covers all of it. beforeNavigate turns the next navigation into a full page load when updated.current says a new build was deployed, so no chunk from the old build is ever requested.

Two decisions in that block. The toaster is unstyled, with class names that base.css dresses as the same tier-3 surface as a dialog, and it moves by screen size: on a phone the bottom of the screen is where the stop sheet opens, so toasts sit under the header instead, offset further when the deploy banner is up there too; on a wide screen they take the free bottom-right corner. svelte-sonner reads a separate mobileOffset below 600px and ignores offset there, so the same value goes to both — without it a phone’s toast sat 16px from the top, over the brand — and the value names the top alone, because a single string would push the sides in by a header’s height as well. Successes are toast.success(…), so they wear a Phosphor check in --ok; errors a warning circle in --coral; the list sits on --z-toast. MediaQuery makes the placement a value the props read rather than a listener. And the cross-fade is CSS on the view-transition pseudo-elements — the old page leaves in 120ms, the new one arrives in 200ms — with the header excluded: it has a view-transition-name of its own and its group is told not to animate, so the one element that should feel fixed does not fade with every page. The trip title morphs over --dur-4; the trip panel rises 4px. All of it also sits inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference — the second lock on a door the script has already locked, since under reduced motion there is no transition for the CSS to style, and a navigation is a cut.

The one load that returns data, and what it returns is about the shell, not a page. (There are two more loads in the project, and neither carries anything for a component to show: the (app) group’s guard, below, and the guide page’s in chapter 36, which picks a prerendered file by its slug.) Identity is needed by every page and by the header around them, which is exactly the case a layout load exists for; the theme cookie is read here for the one picture with two prints (chapter 23), because the server has to choose its sources before any script runs. Everything page-specific comes through remote functions. The (app) group inside (site) adds a second layout load that redirects strangers to sign in — chapter 34 quotes it — so a page under it cannot forget to check. The layout takes its props as LayoutProps from ./$types: the type SvelteKit generates for *this* layout, which knows that data has a user and a theme because the load beside it returned them, and that children is the snippet of the page inside. Every layout in the project types its props that way, and every page with a params or data uses its twin, PageProps (chapter 26). The one effect in the layout is about the device, not the page: whenever it finds nobody signed in, it deletes the copies of pages the service worker kept for reading offline, because they were rendered for whoever was signed in before — chapter 39 says which ways a session can end and why this is the net under all of them.

The header

Two small Svelte 5 things. scrollY from svelte/reactivity/window is the window’s scroll position as a reactive value with the listener managed for us — undefined on the server, where there is no window — and one $derived turns it into the border that appears when the page has scrolled. {const} is a declaration tag: a value computed in the markup and visible to its siblings and their children. It is what Svelte 5.56 put in place of {@const}, which still compiles but is legacy. The two are easy to confuse, and the difference is the whole lesson. {@const} could only sit directly inside a block, and it was *reactive*: the compiler made it a derived value, worked out again whenever what it read changed. A declaration tag works anywhere in the markup, can be a let holding $state, and is reactive only when it says so. A bare one is worked out once, when the block is created; to follow what it reads it wraps the value in $derived, as a const in a <script> would. So the one-for-one translation of old code is {@const x = y} → {const x = $derived(y)}, which is what Svelte’s own documentation gives. Dropping the @ alone gives you the bare, once-only form — and this project made exactly that slip three times, in the header, the diagnostics page and the settings page, each found by a reader noticing something did not update. The link list depends on whether somebody is signed in, and the header sits in the layout, so it outlives a sign-in. The first version was a bare {const}: after signing in there was no “Trips” link until a reload, and after signing out the link stayed. The sign-up test in chapter 46 now looks for it both ways. The header is the only place that needs the list, so it lives where it is used.

Mobile first: the nav is a sheet under the header, opened by a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls, and at forty-eight ems it becomes a row and the button disappears. Below that it behaves like the dialog it is: inert on the page behind it, a scrim that dims the page as every other overlay does, focus moved in and back, Escape to close, and afterNavigate to close it whatever caused the navigation. The scrim is rendered after the <header>, not inside it: the header’s backdrop-filter makes it the containing block of anything fixed inside it, so a scrim in there could not reach the bottom of the screen. And open is an assignable $derived that reads the 48em query: cross the line — an iPad turned to landscape with the sheet open — and it derives afresh, closed, so the page is never left inert behind a menu button that has disappeared. The header is also the same on every page. The first version left out whatever the page already was — no “New trip” on the trips list, no “Sign in” on the sign-in page — and the result was a header whose links, language switcher and theme toggle jumped 130px sideways on the most travelled path in the app, from the trips list into a trip. Now the action is always there, and on its own page it carries aria-current="page", like a nav link: a screen reader says “current page”, and the stylesheet can mark it without a second rule for the same idea. Signing out is a <form> spread from a remote form with no fields, so it works with JavaScript off; with it on, the form’s enhance empties this device’s offline copies before the submission ends the session (chapter 39). The end-to-end helper in chapter 46 has to know about the sheet, which is the kind of thing a phone project in the test matrix catches. And every href in it is a call to href() — the next section — so the link list is a list of typed route ids, /(site)/(app)/trips and friends, not strings that happen to look like paths.

Why class={[…]}, and not class:nav--open={open}

A class that comes and goes is written in this project as the class attribute with an array or an object in it: class={['nav', { 'nav--open': open }]} — strings are always there, an object’s keys are there while their values are truthy, and Svelte turns the lot into one string with the same rules as the clsx library. Before Svelte 5.16 the convenient way was the class: directive, one per class: class="nav" class:nav--open={open}. It still compiles, and Svelte’s documentation now says to prefer the attribute, because the attribute is one value — it can be built in the script, passed as a prop, and merged with a class handed in from outside, class={['btn', props.class]}, none of which a directive can do. You will meet the directive in older code and in libraries; read it as the same thing written the earlier way.

One way to write a link

A dozen lines of code under three dozen of comment, and the comment is the point. resolve() from $app/paths is SvelteKit’s typed link: the route id — groups included, which is why it is /(site)/(app)/trips/new and not /trips/new — is checked against the routes that exist, the parameters against the matchers in src/params.ts, and since 2.54 — resolve() itself is from 2.26; the search-string form came later, so every 3.x has it — the id may carry its own search string or hash, so href(/(site)/t/[slug=slug]?tab=${tab}, { slug }) is one call and still typed. Paraglide’s localizeHref then puts the language in front. Wrapping the two in one function means a link cannot forget either half: rename a folder and every link to it is a type error in every component; add a language and every link already speaks it.

The return type is ResolvedPathname, and that is not a trick played on the linter — on one condition, which vite.config.ts sets: paths.relative: false. With SvelteKit’s default, true, resolve() answers a *server* render with a path relative to the page, ./explore or ../trips, so the HTML still works if the whole app is moved under a subdirectory; Paraglide’s localizeHref then resolved that against an origin and handed back a whole URL, http://localhost:4173/explore. Every link in the server’s HTML carried the build’s origin, and so did every prerendered guide — and the header could not mark the page it was on, because isCurrent compares the page’s pathname with each href, and a URL is never equal to a pathname. Nobody saw it in a browser, which redraws the links as root-relative paths the moment it hydrates; chapter 46 has the test that reads the server’s HTML with JavaScript off. This app is served from the root of its domain, so the portability was worth nothing and the setting is false. SvelteKit defines the type as /${Path} *or* /${string}/${Path} — a slot for a base path in front of every resolved pathname — and /de/trips is exactly that shape, a prefix that reroute in src/hooks.ts strips before routing. eslint-plugin-svelte’s no-navigation-without-resolve rule, which started recognising SvelteKit 3 projects in 3.23.1, accepts an href or a goto() of that type; it cannot see through localizeHref, and this is the honest way to tell it what the wrapper does. The one link in the app that bypasses href() is the language switcher in chapter 21, and it says why in a comment the linter reads.

The footer is product copy, not a build log: one sentence and two links. version from $app/env — the commit hash — is on the element as data-version, so “which build is this?” is answered for whoever opens the inspector, and on the diagnostics page in words, without a hash sitting in front of every visitor. The banner appears when updated.current flips — under the header on a phone, where the toasts also go, never at the bottom where the stop sheet opens — and its button is a plain reload, because there is nothing to save that the server does not already have.

Two error pages, one view

A URL that matches no route lands on the root +error.svelte, inside the root layout, which has no header — so the root error page brings a small one of its own. An error on a site page renders (site)/+error.svelte, inside the site layout, with the full header. Both render ErrorView, so the words live once: the status large in the display face and the secondary grey, over a faint compass rose turned 45° so its points fall between the digits — decoration, so aria-hidden, while the heading carries the meaning — a sentence, two ways out (back to your trips, or explore), and the reference id from handleError when there is one.

Checkpoint

  • You can say why the root layout has no load, and what would go wrong if it did.
  • You can explain what onNavigate and beforeNavigate each do here.
  • You know why there are two +error.svelte files and what each one adds.
